Bar Harbor.wildlife_intro:
Bar Harbor's wildlife problem is the off-season. Grand summer homes, inns and cottages stand closed from fall into late spring with Acadia's forest on every side, and raccoons, bats and gray squirrels move into attics, chimneys and crawl spaces undisturbed. Raccoons are bold around the village and the waterfront, porcupines work the wooded lots, and skunks den under the porches of quiet winter streets. Owners often learn about a winter of occupancy from a caretaker's spring report — or from the smell when they arrive.

Our crew works with owners and caretakers on exactly this pattern: fall sealing before closing, spring inspections at opening, and bat exclusions timed to Maine law, which bars exclusion from unoccupied buildings in June and July. Chimney caps, screened vents and sealed soffits do most of the work here. If your Bar Harbor home sits empty for months, call us to set up a closing and opening routine — it is the surest way to keep the island's wildlife in the park, where it belongs.

Blue Hill.wildlife_intro:
Blue Hill mixes working farms, village homes and summer cottages, and the wildlife follows all three. Raccoons raid barns, feed storage and shoreline trash, bats settle into the attics of older village homes and seasonal cottages, and gray squirrels work the big trees around the harbor straight onto the rooflines. Inland, porcupines chew outbuildings and camp woodwork, groundhogs burrow in the fields and gardens the town is known for, and skunks den under porches through the village. Beavers flood the low roads where streams cross toward the bay.

Summer homes closed for winter are the repeat offenders — animals get nine quiet months and owners get one bad opening weekend. Our crew seals seasonal places in the fall, handles bat colonies by exclusion only under Maine timing rules, and hardens barns and outbuildings for year-round residents. Coastal winters are milder than inland Maine but still long, and a building left unsealed in October is rarely empty by May. Call us for a closing inspection and start the season with a clean house.

Trenton.wildlife_intro:
Trenton guards the causeway to Mount Desert Island, and nearly every animal headed for the island passes through its woods and shoreline first. Raccoons forage the Union River Bay shore and raid homes along Route 3, bats occupy the attics of seasonal cottages and older homes, and gray squirrels and skunks are steady across the shore roads and inland lots. Porcupines work the wooded properties, groundhogs burrow in the open ground and blueberry land, and beavers plug the small streams crossing the rural roads.

Trenton's mix of year-round homes and seasonal places means our crew sees both patterns here: the occupied home that needs a squirrel sealed out this week, and the cottage opened in May to a winter of raccoon damage. Fall sealing is the answer for the second, and a proper full-roofline inspection is the answer for the first. Bat work is exclusion only, timed to Maine rules for unoccupied buildings.
